<!-- Generated by Pixl from the skill "Add to an existing screen so it still looks like one screen", version 1. Edit it in the Skills tab, not here: changes made here are overwritten. -->

## Steps
1. Before writing anything, open the page's HTML, CSS and script. List what it already uses: colours, fonts, corner radius, button classes, the file drop zone, headings, spacing.
2. Build the new part from those same classes and pieces. Copy the existing look; do not invent a second one.
3. Never leave a bare browser control (grey "Choose File" button, default select, plain checkbox). Style it like the matching control on the page, or reuse the existing drop zone.
4. Fit the feature into the ONE screen: a toggle, tabs or a segmented control for modes (for example "2 codes / 3 codes"), not a second copy of the section underneath. One main action per screen.
5. Keep the old behaviour working and visible by default; the new mode must not break it.
6. Give the new part the same states as the old: empty, loading, error and result, with the same wording style and spacing.
## Checklist
- [ ] Same fonts, colours, radius and buttons as the rest of the page.
- [ ] No unstyled browser control anywhere.
- [ ] No section that repeats another one.
- [ ] The old flow still works and its tests still pass.
## Definition of done
A person cannot tell which part was added later, and the page still has one clear main action.
## Verify
Open the page and look (see the skill "Look at your own screen before you call it done"). Run the old tests and the new ones.
## Common mistakes
A second form stacked under the first. A new panel in plain HTML next to styled ones. New wording that does not match the buttons around it.
## Example
Adding "compare three codes" to a two-code page: a "2 codes / 3 codes" toggle above the same drop zones, a third zone that appears in 3 mode, and the same Compare button.
